en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Vuttodaya:
Chapter One—The Exposition of the Designation of Consonants.
Homage to the Triple Gem!

May there be success for the world! Homage to the Lord of Sages, who destroys the darkness within the mental continuum of beings, whose radiant light shines forth with the brilliance of the Dhamma, and who is pure and resplendent.

That meter which was formerly delighted by the teacher Piṅgalācārya and others does not achieve the desired purity of the Magadha dialects, whether it is intended as such or not intended as such by the poet. (Ka.)
Next, the measurement of the text, the classification of measures and phonemes in the Māgadhī language,
together with the definitions and characteristics, and the sequence of words whose meanings are clear.
This work called Vuttodaya, which depends on worldly meter,
I shall now begin for the sake of the easy understanding of those [who seek it], starting from the definitions and so forth.

The conventions for prosodic feet (*gaṇa*) are as follows: *sabbaglamnā* (all long), *digalahū* (first and last short), *bhyā* (first and second short), *majjha’nta garū* (middle and final long), *jasā* (second and third long), *majjha’ntalā* (middle and final short),
*ra* (first and third short), *te’te’ṭṭha* (all short), *go* (all long), *garu* (long), and *lo* (short).
The rule for the *gaṇa* (group) is: *bha*, *ja*, *sā*; all [the remaining syllables] are light. These five are established as *gaṇas*;
they are to be understood starting from the noble (*ariya*) [meter], where a *gaṇa* here consists of four beats.
A syllable is heavy when it consists of a conjunct consonant and so forth, or when it is long, or when followed by a *niggahīta*;

likewise, a syllable is heavy if it is "crooked" (containing a *vaṅka* vowel) or ends in a consonant (*pādanta*). Any other syllable is light, being "straight" (*uju*) and measured by a single *mātrā*.
In the combination of *pāda*s and so forth, a preceding heavy syllable is in some cases to be understood as light; an example of this is as follows:
"This generation, bound by craving, [is intent] upon the experience of the taste of seeing the Victor."
O disciplined one, what action does not produce wonder?
Perception is to be understood from the world, as in the case of the ocean and its saltiness and so forth;
the foot is to be known as the fourth part, while the division of words constitutes the meter.
It is said to be of three kinds: *sama* (even), *maḍḍhasama* (half-even), and *visama* (uneven).
That whose feet are even according to their characteristics is *sama*.
That in which the second [foot] is equal to the last, and the first is equal to the third, is *maḍḍhasama*.
However, one should consider that the *Taḍadḍhasama* and others possess distinct characteristics for each quarter (*pāda*).
Starting from a single syllable up to twenty-six syllables per quarter,
that meter is declared by various names accordingly.
*Daṇḍaka*, *caṇḍavutthi*, and so forth—these are [designated] by six feet, but by three;
and likewise in other treatises, the term "gāthā" is used. Thus, the designation for *chandas* (meter) has been explained.
Furthermore, that which was mentioned immediately prior is another [type]; this is the commonality based on name.
"In the words of the Lord of Sages, it is designated simply as 'Gāthā.
However, by taking certain specific names that are entirely appropriate here, I shall show them to you; they will also serve as titles."
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Exposition of Technical Terms and Definitions," in the *Chandaso-saññā-paribhāsā-niddesa* [Exposition of Grammatical Signs and Rules] within the *Udaya*. 2.
The Second Chapter:
The Exposition of the Measure of Syllables (*Mātrāvuttiniddesa*)
The sixth rule for gaṇas:
[the first gaṇa] may be either all-light (lll) or light-and-heavy (l-);
the others are six heavy [syllables], and no [gaṇa] is light-in-the-odd [position].
In the noble [verse], *anta* is the sixth; in the *go*, *gaṇa* is the sixth, and the others are different.
In the first half of the *yatiniyama*, if the sixth is [the *gaṇa*],...
If it contains all the vowels, it is called *itthā’dila*;
if it contains those [vowels] with *r*, it is *antepi*; if it contains them even at the end, it is *carimepi*, and the fourth is at the end.
19. If the noble state of recluseship (*ariyasāmañña*) exists, its characteristic is as previously stated.
20. That [verse] whose first pair of feet is identical to its shoulders is called *pathyā*.
Where three groups exceed [the standard], and the first [group] occurs in both places, it is *vipulā*.
22. The letter *ja* occurs in the middle of the *garu* (heavy) syllables, and the fourth and second [syllables] are *capalā*.
If the *capalā* occurs throughout, and that [verse] possesses this initial characteristic, while possessing another characteristic of *pathyā*, it is called *mukhacapalā*.
If the characteristic of *pathyā* is found in the first half,
but that of *capalā* in the second half, and then in the second leaf [of the second half], that which is thus described is *jaghanacapalā*. These are the noble (*ariya*) meters.
If all [the feet] are in the first circle, or if the characteristics stated for both [circles] apply to the syllables in the circles of whichever [verse],
that is called a *gīti*; the *lalitā* is said to have the same metrical pause (*yati*).
In this second half of the noble [Upagīti], whatever has been stated as the complete definition applies to both halves; if it is so for both,
then that is indeed called an Upagīti.
The Noble One’s pair of halves possesses the characteristics previously stated;
that in which the opposite occurs is here called "fire."
If the first half-verse consists of noble (ariyā) syllables and the second half is joined with one additional heavy (garu) syllable at the end,
or if the other half is equal to the first half, this is called the *ariyāgīti*. These are the types of *gīti* meters.
In the uneven [pādas], there should be six *kalās* in the opening;
in the even [pādas], there are eight, consisting of *ra*, *la*, *ga*.
After that, it is called *Vetālīya*; in the even [pādas], there is no uninterrupted sequence of six short syllables (*laghus*).
That which has the *vetālīya* meter in its first half and the *opacchandasaka* meter (*ra, ya,
ya*) at the end is called *āpātalikā*, provided the other [half] is as before. 31.
When one stands with all four feet placed firmly,
facing toward the south from the beginning,
that is called "the northern course."
And that which is established in the uneven [feet] here: 34.
If *ga* or *jā* occurs in the even [feet], it is declared to be "reversion" (*paccavutti*).
The *sama* and *asama* [feet] are equal in their initial syllables.
She is joined with that which causes it to proceed. 36. Her end is made even.
37. Then another, with a lovely smile.
The *Vetālīya* meters. 38.
*Dvikavihata-vasu-laghu-acala-dhṛti-riha*. 39. *Mattāsamaka*:
the ninth [syllable] is *la-ga* at the end.

If there is a *citā* in the fifth, eighth, or ninth *loka*.
43. Ga: If this [verse] is further embellished by eight [syllables], it is called *Citrā*.
That which possesses the specific characteristics of the past [metres] and has feet expressed with measures such as *mattā* and *samā*, is called *Visiloka*.
The *Aniyata* [meter] is said to be accompanied by a fixed measure;
the *Vānavāsikā*, the *Pādākulaka* recited among people (*visiloka*),
and the *Mattāsamaka* are types of meters.
Without vowels there are only morae; without heavy syllables, however, there are only vowels;
without light syllables, there are only heavy syllables. These are considered the components of the *pathyā* and other meters.
Thus ends the section titled "The Exposition of Morae" in the *Vuttodaya*, a treatise on prosody.

this is *Bṛhatī*.

If it is *campakamālā*, it consists of *bha*, *ma*, *sā*, and *go*; this is stated again solely for the purpose of indicating a different name (*nāmantara*) [according to the Ṭīkā].

61. If that *ta* is followed by *ma*, *rā*, or *lca*, it is called *ubbhāsaka*.
62. When *to* is followed by *jā* or a heavy (*garu*) vowel, this is established as the *panti* [meter].
63. *Indravajrā* consists of *ta*, *ja*, *ra*, *ja*, *ga*, *ga*.
64. *Upendravajrā* consists of *u*, *pa*, *ta*, *ja*, *ta*, *ja*, *ga*, *ga*.
If it possesses the characteristics just described [in the preceding verse], it is [called] *Upendravajrā*.
When the feet are mixed, they are *upajāti*s;
(Indravajrā) thus it is said that even when others are mixed, (Indravajrā) they call them by this very name, *jāti*. (Upendravajrā)
66. *Sumukhī* is said to consist of *na*, *ja*, *ja*, *la*, and *g*. 67.
If one desires *Dodhaka*, there should be *bha*, *bha*, *bha*, and *g*. 68.
That which is composed of *tga*, *ga*, *sa*, *la*, *na*, *sa*, *la*, and *ga* is *Sālinī*.

*Lalitā* is said by the wise to consist of *ta*, *bha*, *ja*, and *ra*.
83. That which consists of short syllables, with *ja*, *sa*, and *se* following an *uditta* accent, is [the Vṛttamālā].
84. That which is accompanied by *na*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, and *sa* is declared to be the Ujjalā.
85. Its five feet are unbroken; that which has *ma*, *ma*, and *ya* is the Vessadevī.

87. When they are *sa*, *ya*, and *sa* with a *ya*, it is to be known as *kamalā*;
this is *jagatī*.
88. *Mnā jrā go*, [and] that [meter] is called *Tridaśayatipraharsinī*.
89. With four *ganas* here, [the meter] *Rucirā* has *ja-bha-sja-ga*.
It is *Atijagatī*.
90. *Aparājitā* consists of na, na, ra, sa, a light syllable (laghu), and the gaṇas gā and sarehi. 91. *Praharṇakalikā* is defined as na, na, bha, na, la, and gi.
92. *Vasantatilakā* is said to consist of ta, bha, ja, ja, ga, and go.
93. *Sakkarī*:
two *hata* (eight syllables), light (*laghu*), *ratha* (six syllables), *gi* (one syllable), and *ti* (one syllable); it has a crescent moon (*sasikalā*) [at its end].
94. *Vasu* (eight), *haya* (seven), and *yati* (caesura) at *ri* (two syllables), *ha* (one syllable), *maṇiguṇanikara*.
95. This *mālinī* consists of [the feet] ending in *na, na, ma, ya, ya*, with *yutā* (two *ya*s) and *bhogi* (four *i*s).
96. When it consists of *na, ja, bha, ja* and is endowed with *rasa* (six *ga*s), it is *pabhaddakaṃ*.
It is an *atisakkari*.
97. When the syllables na, ja, bha, ja, and rā always occur, joined by a *ga*, it is the *Aṭṭhi* meter. 98.
When the sequence ya, ma, na, sa, bha, la, ga, with pauses at the sixth and seventh syllables, it is the *Sikhariṇī* meter.
99. *Rasa*, *yugi*, *sito*, *no so mrā slā*—when there are [the syllables] *gya’dā hariṇī*, then it is [called] *tadā*.
100. *Mandakkantā*: *ma, bha, na, ta, ta, gā*; *go yugu, tva, ssakehi*.
This is *Accaṭṭhi*.
101. The movement of her arms was like flowering creepers, indeed, because of the tremors of her limbs.
*Dhuti*. 102.

That which is stated as being of this kind by name has the sequence *ra*, *jā*, *ra*, *jā*, *ra*, *jā*, with heavy and light syllables.

Pakati.

4. The Fourth Chapter: Exposition of the Half-Equal Metre.
If that [metre] has *sa*, *la*, *ga* in the uneven [pādas], and [the same] in the even [pādas]...
For one who is respectful, there is weightiness and merit.
If the verses are recited quickly or at a medium pace by one who is respectful, they do not become inferior.
If it has three syllables with a heavy (guru) [syllable] at the end,
and if the *vegavatī* has three syllables with a light (laghu) [syllable] at the end;
if "to" and "jo" are used, and there is a heavy syllable in the uneven [pādas].

In the *ākhyānakī* meter, there are *ja*, *ga*, *ga*, and *go* in the odd feet;

(Indravajra) In the even feet, however, there are *ja*, *ta*, *ja*, *ga*, and *go*. (Upendravajra) In the odd feet there are *ja*, *ta*, *ja*, *ga*, and *go*, but in the even feet it is the same as [the previous]; (Upendravajra)

and if one desires the *aparavaktra* meter at that time;
and if there are *na*, *na*, *ra*, *ya*; it is irregular (*viṣama*).
Na, ja, ja, ra, ga, and samaka with a blossoming opening—

123. [The vowel] *e* occurs in *seta*, *vassa*, and so on, in all cases. 124. [The vowel] *o* occurs in *bhe*, *na*, *aṇṇavā*, *bha*, *abbi*, and *pulā*. 125.

This is the classification of the *vatta* [meter].

If that which is not seen in the *chanda* [meter] is seen in the *payoga* [application], it is a verse (*gāthā*) characterized by irregular syllables and feet; this is the section on irregular meters within the *Vuttodaya*, under the general heading of prosody.
Thus ends the description of irregular meters in the *Vuttodaya*.
The Fifth Chapter.
6. The Sixth Chapter on the Analysis of the Six Conditions: The Method of Exposition (Paṭṭhānanaya).
In the *patthāra* (spreading out), all feet are equal, with the first foot below and the others above;
those [feet] are heavy in the first position, and these [subsequent ones] should be arranged until all possibilities are exhausted. This is the method for the lost (*naṭṭha*).
If there should be a missing digit, when that [digit] is added, it becomes even;
but when it is uneven, it becomes odd when one is added. When added, it becomes heavy. This is the method for the enumeration.
In the sequence beginning with one, write the numbers below the first [digit] in double value;
when combined with the light syllables, it becomes the *uddiṭṭhaka* [method].
This is the method for all syllable-operations (*galakriya*).
The number is equal to the stated syllables; the writing is one by one above and below. Each successive term is reduced by one, starting from one;
in the case of "nu" (the base), it begins with all [syllables] and so forth. This is the method for calculating the stated numbers.
In the *Sandoha* of the *Garukriyā-aṅka*, when the number is mixed, the sum of the stated numbers is called *eko ve*;
this is the method for bringing them together. This concludes the section on the reduction of what has been stated.
The number itself is doubled and reduced by one for the width, arising from the length;
and half of what has been stated is the finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) for the intermediate spaces and for the Garuḷas.
Thus ends the section on the analysis of the six suffixes in the *Vuttodaya* prosody.
The Sixth Chapter:
Conclusion.
To the Elder Sīla, who dwelt in the Āyatana monastery within the Sela cave.
This foot of mine, which honors virtues,
is victorious; for by relying upon its power,
even I have accomplished this desired benefit that brings success to others.
By means of the merit I have attained through accomplishing the welfare of others, may I,
in birth after birth, become one who accomplishes the welfare of others.
Just as the six conditions were fulfilled by me merely by looking down.
"Those who have achieved [their goal] surely help others achieve it,
even when the meaning is wrongly conceived by living beings. Thus ends the treatise *Vuttodaya*,
composed by the Great Elder Saṅgharakkhita.
